name: FastAccounting
shortBlurb: Group suggestions for each Tally entry, trained on an accounting firm's books across 5 companies, with a person reviewing every suggestion.
tagline: Suggests the party and expense group for every Tally entry, from each company's own books.
seoTitle: FastAccounting: ML for Tally Expense Groups
metaDescription: FastAccounting suggests party and expense groups for Tally daybook entries, flags unusual ones and forecasts recurring expenses, with a model per company.
description: FastAccounting suggests the party group and the expense group for each entry in a Tally daybook. It was trained on an accounting firm's books: 5 companies, 60 months and about 48,000 transactions. Each company gets its own pair of models, because each firm names its groups and vendors in its own way. The system takes a Tally daybook export in CSV, turns exported expenses into positive values, maps group names to one spelling, and drops voucher IDs and entry numbers before training. Ledger names and narrations are read as text, which copes with the spelling variants vendor names pick up over time. The Streamlit app is built to show the top suggestions with a confidence score. The design also covers a forecast of recurring expenses and an anomaly model that flags unusual entries for a person to check first. A person reviews every suggestion, and the design posts nothing to the books on its own.

name: CallMind
shortBlurb: Hindi call recordings transcribed, labelled and scored against each campaign's script, for a national education NGO's calling team.
tagline: Every Hindi call scored against its campaign script, with the evidence shown beside each score.
metaDescription: CallMind transcribes Hindi call recordings, labels the caller and teacher, and scores each call against its campaign script.
description: CallMind turns recorded Hindi calls into compliance reports. Each recording goes to Sarvam, a hosted Hindi speech service, which transcribes the call and separates the 2 speakers, labelled CALLER and TEACHER. Every campaign has a script, and the script becomes a rule set: a list of rules, each with the phrases a caller should say. A manager uploads the script, an LLM drafts the rules and a word list, and a named approver edits the draft and publishes it. Only a person can publish, and a published version is locked in the database. The scorer then checks each rule against the transcript and runs the compliance and call-flow checks alongside the script score. Every rule result keeps the phrase it matched and the time in the call where it was said, so a supervisor can play the recording beside the transcript and check where the score came from. Scoring covers every call that has a script, and each campaign's scores follow its published rule set. When a new version is published, older runs stay visible. CallMind was built for a national education NGO's calling team, and a pilot is running there.

name: JNVessays
shortBlurb: Scores scanned handwritten essays against a 4-part rubric, on a local model with no cloud API.
tagline: First-pass essay scores from scanned handwriting, for a teacher to check.
metaDescription: JNVessays reads scanned handwritten essays with OCR and scores each one on a 4-part rubric, using a local model with no cloud API.
description: JNVessays gives a teacher a first-pass score for each handwritten essay, scored on a 4-part rubric. Each essay is scanned as a single image, saved as a JPG or JPEG and named by its submission ID. EasyOCR reads English handwriting into text, and Tesseract takes over on any file where EasyOCR fails. The text then goes to a small local language model, llama3.2:3b, run through Ollama. The prompt carries 4 worked examples, and the model returns a score and a 1-line reason for each criterion. The criteria are content (the topics a student covers), cohesion (grammar and spelling), coherence (structure and flow) and simplicity (sentence clarity). Each criterion scores 0, 0.5 or 1, for a total out of 4. Code checks every result for the right shape and allowed values. It flags what fails and keeps the result for review. Each score takes its ID from the essay's own file, so it stays with that essay. The scoring model runs on the same machine as the rest of the pipeline, and no cloud API is called. An evaluator sets the AI scores beside the teacher's scores for the same essays. The design keeps the teacher in charge of every final mark, and the reading step is designed for multilingual essays.

name: DocIntel
shortBlurb: MCA filings in, due-diligence Word and Excel reports out, for a Mumbai regulatory due-diligence firm.
tagline: Reads MCA company filings, from scanned PDFs to fillable forms, and builds the due-diligence report from them.
metaDescription: DocIntel reads MCA filings (AOC-4, MGT-7, DIR-12 and more) from scanned, digital and fillable PDFs, and builds Word and Excel due-diligence reports.
description: DocIntel reads the company filings that Indian companies submit to the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA) and turns them into the reports a due-diligence team works from. A Mumbai regulatory due-diligence firm, which checks companies for private equity funds, AIFs and NBFCs, runs it with its own team on 2,000+ documents a month. Each company comes with a folder of filings: annual returns, financial statements, incorporation papers and director filings. DocIntel recognises each filing's type (MGT-7, AOC-4, DIR-12, ADT-1 and others) and reads it the right way. Fillable forms give up their field values directly and skip OCR. Scanned pages are read with OCR on a GPU, and digital PDFs are read as text. Messy text, such as director lists, goes to a language model, with a rules-based fallback if the model call fails. Every filing for one company is processed in one run, and the output is a Word report plus 2 Excel sheets, one for financials and one for shareholding. OCR and the language model run on cloud GPU servers, and the firm's analysts check every report before it goes to the investor. It's built to check figures across a company's filings, so a mismatch in one shows up against the others.

name: GradeQP
shortBlurb: Checks MBA question papers against University of Mumbai paper-setting rules and cites the rule behind each finding.
tagline: Checks a draft question paper against its university's rules, with the rule behind every finding.
metaDescription: GradeQP checks draft MBA question papers against University of Mumbai rules, cites the rule behind each finding and returns a verdict before moderation.
description: GradeQP checks a draft question paper against its university's paper-setting rules before the paper goes to moderation. The setter uploads a Word or PDF draft. The text is parsed, with OCR for scanned pages, and one structured LLM call turns it into a header, questions, sub-parts, marks and course-outcome tags. The subject in the header selects a course rulebook. If no rulebook matches, the report says so and the setter picks the course, so nothing is checked against a guessed rulebook. Eight exact checks run in code on total marks, duration, question count and tags. Judgement rules run as separate LLM calls, in parallel with them. For pick-N papers, the total check adds the compulsory marks to the best N optional marks, so a compliant paper passes. The verdict is Ready, Needs changes or Could not fully verify, and a mandatory rule that can't run sets the verdict to Could not fully verify. Every finding cites its rule. For a Word draft, the setter also gets a copy of the file with comments on the affected questions. The rulebooks cover 10 MMS Semester I subjects, built on 4-credit and 2-credit paper templates.

name: Report Copilot
shortBlurb: Self-serve state reports with masked teacher details, and identified lists only after approval, for a national education NGO.
tagline: Self-serve reports for state teams, with teacher details masked until a named approver signs off.
seoTitle: Report Copilot: Masked Reports for NGOs
metaDescription: State teams download their own reports with teacher names and phones masked. Real names appear only on an identified list, after an approver signs off.
description: Report Copilot is a report portal for a national education NGO's state teams. Staff pick one of 7 report types for their state and download it as a PDF or Excel file. Access is set by state, and a user sees only the states they hold. Programme data lands in BigQuery through Airbyte, and every column is classified against a reviewed list of 1,763 columns. A column missing from that list stops the warehouse run before any row moves. The warehouse is built to mask teacher names and phone numbers when it builds its tables, so report scripts read masked values only. Each report is a fixed script with its own tests, checked against the NGO's existing Power BI figures, and users can't ask for new SQL through the portal. When someone needs real names, they raise a disclosure request with a reason. A named approver signs off before any identified list is built. The database blocks anyone from approving their own request, and every request, decision and release is logged with the file's expiry date. Before a PDF goes out, a release check reads it back and confirms that each teacher's name prints correctly. The portal holds no warehouse credential, only a token for the report service. The report service runs on 1 server in India, and the NGO's own team runs the portal, which ships with 1,162 automated tests.

name: Valent
shortBlurb: Reads charters and cap tables, finds the preference terms that set payout order, and ties every value to its source sentence.
tagline: Every preference term tied to its source sentence, and confirmed by a person before any payout runs.
metaDescription: Valent extracts liquidation preference terms from charters and articles, ties each value to its source sentence, and runs payout maths on confirmed terms.
description: Valent reads a company's charter and cap table and finds the preference terms that decide who gets paid first when the company is sold. The model proposes each term with a verbatim quote, and a citation check looks for that quote in the source. A value with no matching quote halts the run, so nothing unverified reaches a payout. A reviewer confirms or corrects every term on a review screen, including each seniority rank, and only confirmed terms feed the payout engine. For Delaware charters and cap tables, the engine works out what each class receives at an exit value you set. It checks every combination of converting or holding each preferred series and returns the stable outcome, because one series' choice changes everyone else's payout. The simulator shows the payout at any exit value and runs on confirmed terms only. The cap table is built to export to Excel. Indian articles of association go through the same extraction and citation path, from text PDFs, XFA forms and scanned filings after OCR. Articles set out the preference terms, and the shareholdings sit in a cap table, so Indian payouts need shareholding data. Fair market value needs an EV-to-equity bridge and a locked valuation date, which sit outside the tool. Documents and extracted terms are stored in Postgres. Clause text goes to the model you configure, which is OpenRouter by default or a local Ollama model, and every model call is traced in Langfuse.

name: Contract Risk Radar
shortBlurb: Clause-by-clause review of supplier contracts against 133 policy obligations, built for a global energy and automation company.
tagline: Every supplier clause checked against your own policy, with a verdict and the rule behind it.
seoTitle: Contract Risk Radar: AI Contract Review
metaDescription: Contract Risk Radar checks each supplier contract clause against your policy library, flags what weakens or breaks a rule, and drafts fixes from past reviews.
description: Contract Risk Radar reads a supplier contract clause by clause and checks every clause against the company's own policy obligations. We built it for a global energy and automation company, which runs it on its real supplier contracts and owns what we built. The policy library (terms and conditions, security rules and a data protection agreement) is read once and turned into a checklist of 133 obligations. Each new contract is split into clauses, and each clause is checked against each obligation. Every flagged clause gets a status (Present, Weakened, Contradicted or Absent) and a verdict (Accept, Modify, Replace, Reject or Escalate). The system learns from the company's own history: past reviewer decisions are stored as examples, and each clause is matched to the closest ones. Replacement wording appears only for Modify or Replace verdicts, only at medium or high confidence, and only where a past decision supplies the text. Every result is checked against a fixed schema before it's saved, and the model runs at temperature 0, built so a re-run of the same contract gives the same findings. The model runs on a dedicated virtual machine with a GPU that the company contracts. Only the company's security team can see the contracts and findings. The reviewer gets a screen with every finding, and keeps the final call.

name: Farm Wildlife Alerts
shortBlurb: Camera-based crop-raider alerts that name the animal and stay quiet for livestock, dogs and people.
tagline: A night watch for crop plots that names the animal: deer, monkey or wild boar raise an alert, and everything else stays silent.
seoTitle: Farm Wildlife Alerts: Night Crop Raiders
metaDescription: A camera watches a crop plot at night, names the animal (deer, monkey or wild boar) and alerts the farmer with the photo. Try the public demo.
description: Farm Wildlife Alerts watches a crop plot through a camera and decides, frame by frame, whether a crop-raiding animal has walked in. It detects every animal in the frame, classifies each one into 1 of 11 classes, and raises an alert for deer, monkey or wild boar. Livestock, dogs, jackals, peafowl, small mammals, people, nilgai and empty frames are known silent classes, so the system stays quiet for them. Each alert carries the frame, so the farmer can see what's in the field before going out. Video gets a motion check first, so the heavier models only run when something moves. If a file can't be checked, the system reports "could not check", and a fault shows up as a warning. Every model file is checked against a recorded fingerprint at start-up, and the live pipeline matches the trained one step for step. It runs on a GPU server in our own office, and a public demo page lets anyone upload a photo or video and see the result. Night is the design focus: the night classifier is built to separate cattle from deer in infrared frames, and nilgai alerts come next.

name: LeapBuddy

description: LeapBuddy is a chat assistant that answers a national education NGO's teacher-entrepreneurs from the NGO's own material: the programme FAQ, teaching text, worksheets and training videos. Each answer draws only on those sources. If the material doesn't cover a question, the assistant says so and doesn't guess. Every message passes a safety check before any model call runs. A risk match gets a fixed reply, and a staff team is alerted in a private Slack channel. Any other question is sorted into one of 8 departments, such as Product Management or Classroom Management, and searched across catalog videos, teaching text and FAQ rows. A team-approved answer that closely matches the question leads. The assistant then picks one action: answer from text, answer with a video link, ask a clarifying question, decline as out of scope, or escalate. The reply is written from the top 4 sources only, and any link outside those sources is removed. A request for a test or homework gets worksheets and practice sheets, never a video. Every turn is logged, and every model call is traced in Langfuse. LeapBuddy's pilot is under way as a web chat, with teachers and WhatsApp next.

name: TreadCycle
shortBlurb: Machine learning and forecasting that infers when owners replace their tyres, from fitment sales and replacement registrations.
tagline: When each segment replaces its tyres, and how sure the model is.
metaDescription: A proof of concept that infers when car owners replace their tyres, from fitment sales and warranty registrations, with a Gaussian mixture model per segment.
description: TreadCycle estimates when car owners replace the tyres fitted on their new cars. We built it as a proof of concept for a tyre manufacturer, on its own data: tyre fitment sales by car model from 2015 to 2024, and replacement warranty registrations from 2021 to 2024. There's no direct record of tyre life, so the model infers it. Each year's replacements are shared across the fitment years 1 to 9 years earlier, in proportion to the tyres fitted in each year. A Gaussian mixture model per car maker and vehicle type then finds the replacement patterns (early replacers, the main group and delayers) where an average would show 1 number. 11 segments had enough data for a model, and each one showed 2 to 4 patterns. The work also showed the limit of the data: replacements are recorded for only 4 years, so early fitment years show only their long lags. We built a censored joint fit to correct for that and tested it on synthetic data, and the next phase needs replacement records that link back to the fitted vehicles. A dashboard, built for the client's team, shows which segments to reach first and in which year.
